questions.question: Which city is scheduled to host the Summer Olympic Games 2024?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Paris**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The 2024 Summer Olympics**, officially known as the Games of the XXXIII Olympiad, are scheduled to be held in **Paris, France**. This makes Paris the host city for the event.
 
• Paris was selected as the host city during the **131st IOC Session** held in **2017**. The decision was part of a dual award process where Los Angeles was awarded the 2028 Summer Olympics.
 
• This marks the third time Paris will host the Summer Olympics. It previously hosted the Games in **1900** and **1924**. This makes Paris one of the very few cities to host the Olympics three times. *Hence, the correct answer is Paris.*
 
• **The Paris 2024 Olympics** will take place from **26th July to 11th August 2024**. The event will feature athletes from across the globe competing in various sports disciplines.
 
• The Paris Olympics are expected to emphasize **environmental sustainability**, with a focus on reducing the event's carbon footprint. For example, many existing venues will be utilized to minimize infrastructure development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Paris as a Host City:**

 
 
• **Paris** is the capital city of **France** and is globally recognized for its rich cultural and historical heritage.
 
• Hosting the Olympics in 2024 aligns with the city’s strategic plan to promote sports, culture, and environmental sustainability.
 
• The event will showcase Paris as a global center for innovation and inclusion while preserving its historical significance.
 
 
 
• **Other Host Cities:**
 
 
• **Tokyo**: Hosted the **2020 Summer Olympics**, which were delayed to 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. This was Tokyo's second time hosting the Games, the first being in 1964.
 
• **Los Angeles**: Scheduled to host the **2028 Summer Olympics**. It has previously hosted the Games in 1932 and 1984.
 
• **Beijing**: Hosted the **2008 Summer Olympics** and became the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics (in 2022).
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the Paris 2024 Olympics:**
 
 
• **Sustainability:** Paris aims to organize the most sustainable Olympic Games in history, with a goal to reduce carbon emissions by 50% compared to previous Games.
 
• **Sports Innovation:** For the first time, sports like **breakdancing** will be introduced in the Olympics.
 
• **Venue Utilization:** The majority of the competitions will be held in existing or temporary venues, including iconic Paris landmarks like the **Champs-Élysées** and the **Eiffel Tower**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Significance:**

 
 
• Paris was one of the earliest cities to host the Olympics during the modern Olympic era, highlighting its longstanding association with international sports.
 
• The 2024 Games coincide with the **100-year anniversary** of Paris hosting the 1924 Olympics, making it a highly symbolic event.
 
 
 
• **Economic and Cultural Impact:**
 
 
• Hosting the Olympics is expected to boost Paris’s **economy** through tourism, infrastructure development, and global sponsorships.
 
• The event will also serve as a platform to promote **French culture** and heritage to a global audience.

questions.question: During the water cycle, which part of the plant is involved in the process of evaporation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Leaves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Evaporation in the water cycle:** Evaporation is the process by which water changes from a liquid state to a gaseous state (water vapor). This process is a key component of the water cycle.
 
• **Role of plants:** Plants contribute to evaporation through a process called **transpiration**. Transpiration involves the release of water vapor from plant parts into the atmosphere.
 
• **Leaves:** The **leaves** of plants are primarily responsible for transpiration. Water absorbed by the roots moves up through the plant and is released through tiny openings called **stomata** present on the surface of leaves. Hence, leaves play a crucial role in evaporation during the water cycle.
 
• **Branches, roots, and stems:** While branches, roots, and stems are important for transporting water within the plant, they are not directly involved in the process of evaporation. They function as conduits to deliver water to the leaves. Hence, these parts are not directly responsible for evaporation.
 
• The process of transpiration is vital for maintaining the plant's internal water balance and facilitating nutrient transport. It also contributes to the overall water cycle by releasing water vapor into the atmosphere.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Leaves.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Transpiration:**

 
 
• **Transpiration** is the process by which plants release water vapor into the atmosphere through the stomata in their leaves.
 
• It is estimated that about **10%** of the moisture in the atmosphere is contributed by transpiration from plants.
 
 
 
• **Water cycle:**
 
 
• The **water cycle** is a natural process that involves the continuous movement of water between the earth's surface and the atmosphere.
 
• Key processes include **evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff, and transpiration.**
 
• Transpiration is a significant contributor to evaporation, which forms clouds and eventually leads to rainfall.
 
 
 
• **Stomata:**
 
 
• Stomata are small openings found on the surface of leaves. They facilitate gas exchange and the release of water vapor during transpiration.
 
• The opening and closing of stomata are regulated by **guard cells** based on environmental conditions such as humidity, temperature, and light.
 
 
 
• **Importance of transpiration:**
 
 
• Transpiration helps in **cooling plants**, maintaining water balance, and enabling the transport of nutrients from roots to leaves.
 
• It also contributes to local weather and climate patterns by adding moisture to the air.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Features of transpiration:**

 
 
• Transpiration rate is influenced by factors such as **temperature, humidity, wind speed, and light intensity.**
 
• Plants in arid regions often have adaptations to minimize transpiration, such as **small leaves, thick cuticles, and reduced stomatal density.**
 
 
 
• **Applications of transpiration:**
 
 
• Transpiration plays a vital role in agricultural practices. Monitoring transpiration rates helps in optimizing **irrigation and water management.**
 
• Understanding transpiration dynamics is essential in studying **climate change** and its impact on vegetation and ecosystems.

questions.question: What is an aquifer?

options.text: Saturated zone beneath the water table
Upper surface of the zone of saturation
Lower surface of the saturated zone
Unsaturated zone beneath the water table

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Saturated zone beneath the water table.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An **aquifer** refers to a geological formation capable of holding and transmitting water. It is primarily composed of permeable materials like sand, gravel, or fractured rock.
 
• The term "Saturated zone beneath the water table" is used to define the aquifer because this region is fully saturated with water, meaning all pore spaces between the soil and rock particles are filled with water. *Hence, this is correct.*
 
• The **water table** is the upper boundary of an aquifer, separating the saturated zone from the unsaturated zone above it. *Thus, "Upper surface of the zone of saturation" is not the definition of an aquifer.*
 
• The "Lower surface of the saturated zone" refers to deeper geological layers, which might not always contain usable water or might not transmit water effectively. *This is incorrect.*
 
• The "Unsaturated zone beneath the water table" does not exist because the unsaturated zone is located above the water table. *This is not relevant to the definition of an aquifer.*
 
• **Hydrological significance:** Aquifers are critical for water supply systems as they store and provide water for agricultural, industrial, and domestic uses.
 
• They play a key role in maintaining ecosystems and regulating groundwater flow in natural environments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Aquifers:**

 
 
• **Unconfined Aquifer:** These aquifers are directly connected to the surface and receive water from precipitation and surface sources. The water table defines the upper boundary.
 
• **Confined Aquifer:** These aquifers are bounded by impermeable layers (aquicludes) above and below, and water is under pressure. Wells tapping confined aquifers may exhibit artesian conditions.
 
 
 
• **Uses of Aquifers:**
 
 
• Aquifers serve as a major source of **groundwater**, which is utilized for drinking, irrigation, and industrial purposes.
 
• Many regions depend heavily on groundwater stored in aquifers for sustainable water supply.
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• The **Great Artesian Basin** in Australia is one of the largest and most famous aquifers globally.
 
• The **Ogallala Aquifer** in the United States provides water for agriculture in several states.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• Aquifers are crucial for maintaining the hydrological cycle and supporting environmental balance.
 
• Over-extraction of groundwater from aquifers can lead to problems like **groundwater depletion**, land subsidence, and reduced water quality.
 
• Proper management and conservation of aquifers are essential to prevent issues related to water scarcity.

questions.question: Kalamkari, the traditional art of hand paintings on fabric, originated in which of the following states?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Andhra Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kalamkari** is a traditional Indian art form that involves **hand-painting or block printing** on fabric, particularly using natural dyes.
 
• It originated in the state of **Andhra Pradesh** and is primarily practiced in regions like **Machilipatnam** and **Srikalahasti**.
 
• The term **Kalamkari** is derived from the Persian words **‘kalam’** (pen) and **‘kari’** (craftsmanship), referring to the use of a pen in creating intricate designs.
 
• Srikalahasti style of Kalamkari is known for its **freehand drawing**, while Machilipatnam style often involves **block printing**.
 
• The art form is deeply rooted in **Indian mythology and religious themes**, with motifs often inspired by epics like the **Ramayana** and **Mahabharata**.
 
• Natural dyes are a distinctive feature of Kalamkari; they are derived from sources like **plants, roots, and minerals**.
 
• The traditional process involves treating the fabric with **milk and natural dyes** to prepare it for painting or printing.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Andhra Pradesh.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kalamkari Art Styles:**

 
 
• **Srikalahasti Style:** This style is characterized by **freehand drawing** with a pen and focuses on themes from **Hindu mythology**. Artists use a bamboo pen to draw intricate patterns and figures.
 
• **Machilipatnam Style:** This involves **block printing** using carved wooden blocks and is less intricate than the Srikalahasti style. It often uses **geometric patterns**.
 
 
 
• **Features of Kalamkari:**
 
 
• **Natural Dyes:** The art uses eco-friendly dyes derived from natural sources such as **indigo, turmeric, and pomegranate**.
 
• **Fabric:** Cotton is the most commonly used fabric in Kalamkari, although silk and other materials are also utilized.
 
• **Motifs:** Designs often depict **mythological themes, floral patterns, and animals**.
 
 
 
• **Significance:**
 
 
• Kalamkari holds cultural and spiritual significance, often being used to depict stories from **Indian epics**.
 
• The art form is also a sustainable practice, promoting the use of **natural dyes** and traditional methods.
 
 
 
• **Global Recognition:**
 
 
• Kalamkari has gained international recognition for its **unique craftsmanship** and eco-friendly approach.
 
• It is widely exported and appreciated for its **intricate designs** and **cultural value**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other States and Art Forms:**

 
 
• **Gujarat:** Known for **Patola silk** and **Bandhani tie-dye**.
 
• **Bihar:** Famous for **Madhubani paintings**, another traditional art style.
 
• **Uttar Pradesh:** Renowned for **Chikankari embroidery** and **Zardozi work**.
 
• **Andhra Pradesh:** Apart from Kalamkari, it is also known for **Ikat weaving** and **leather puppetry**.
 
 
 
• **Preservation Efforts:**
 
 
• Government initiatives and NGOs are working to promote and preserve Kalamkari art through **training programs** and **exhibitions**.
 
• Artists are being encouraged to innovate while maintaining traditional methods to ensure the art form's **global appeal**.

questions.question: As of August 2020, India gets its largest export value from:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**refined petroleum**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India's largest export value:** As of **August 2020**, India’s exports primarily constituted refined petroleum products. Refined petroleum accounted for a significant portion of India's export earnings, making it the largest contributor to the country’s export value.
 
• **Refined petroleum:** India is one of the major exporters of refined petroleum in the world. The country refines crude oil and exports products such as diesel, petrol, and jet fuel to various nations.
 
• The refining industry in India is robust, with significant investments in infrastructure and technology. Major refineries are located in states like Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu, which are equipped to process large volumes of crude oil.
 
• **Export destinations:** India exports refined petroleum products to several countries, including **United Arab Emirates, Singapore, China, and the United States**. These nations rely on India for high-quality refined petroleum for industrial and energy purposes.
 
• The export of refined petroleum is vital for India’s economy as it contributes significantly to foreign exchange reserves and helps stabilize the trade deficit.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is refined petroleum.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Refined Petroleum Products:**

 
 
• **Uses:** These products are primarily used in the **transportation sector**, industrial machinery, power generation, and household purposes. Additionally, they are essential in manufacturing plastics and other synthetic materials.
 
• India has a robust refining infrastructure, with some of the largest refineries in the world, such as the **Reliance Industries refinery in Jamnagar, Gujarat**, which is considered the largest refinery globally.
 
• **Spices:** India is renowned for its export of spices such as **turmeric, cardamom, pepper, and cumin**, with major markets in **Europe, the US, and the Middle East**.
 
• **Salt:** India exports salt to countries like **Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Indonesia**, but the value is not as significant as refined petroleum.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic impact of refined petroleum exports:**

 
 
• **Trade deficit reduction:** Petroleum exports help mitigate India’s **trade deficit**, which arises due to large-scale imports of crude oil.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in petroleum exports:**
 
 
• **Environmental concerns:** The refining process and petroleum usage contribute to **carbon emissions**, raising environmental sustainability concerns.

questions.question: Who among the following was a co-founder of the Swaraj Party along with Motilal Nehru?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chittaranjan Das**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chittaranjan Das**, popularly known as **C.R. Das**, was a prominent **freedom fighter, lawyer, and political leader** during the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• He, along with **Motilal Nehru**, co-founded the **Swaraj Party** in **1923**. The main objective of this party was to **achieve self-governance** (Swaraj) for India and oppose colonial policies.
 
• The Swaraj Party was formed as a **political wing** of the Indian National Congress to contest elections and challenge British rule from within the legislative councils.
 
• Chittaranjan Das was the **first President** of the Swaraj Party, while **Motilal Nehru** served as its Secretary. This leadership showcased their commitment to the cause of Indian independence.
 
• C.R. Das is also remembered for his role in defending **Aurobindo Ghosh** in the **Alipore Bomb Case** and for his significant contributions to the **Non-Cooperation Movement** led by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• The Swaraj Party played a vital role in **opposing British policies** in the legislative councils and demanding increased Indian participation in governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other Founders of the Swaraj Party:**

 
 
• **Motilal Nehru:** A leading lawyer and freedom fighter, he played a crucial role in forming the Swaraj Party to demand self-rule and oppose British governance.
 
 
 
• **Features and Objectives of the Swaraj Party:**
 
 
• The Swaraj Party aimed to **contest elections** to the legislative councils established under the Government of India Act, 1919, and use them as platforms to expose British exploitation.
 
• It sought to **disrupt British administration** by opposing unjust laws and policies within the councils.
 
• The party also demanded **increased Indian representation** in governance and greater autonomy for provinces.
 
 
 
• **Other Key Leaders of the Swaraj Party:**
 
 
• **Vithalbhai Patel:** He was a significant member of the Swaraj Party and later became the **President of the Central Legislative Assembly**.
 
• **N.C. Kelkar:** Another prominent member who contributed to the party's efforts to oppose British rule within the councils.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chittaranjan Das:**

 
 
• He was also known as **Deshbandhu** (Friend of the Nation) for his dedication to the Indian independence movement.
 
• Chittaranjan Das passed away in **1925**, but his contributions to the Swaraj Party and the freedom struggle continue to be remembered and honored.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of the Swaraj Party:**
 
 
• Though the Swaraj Party declined after the death of Chittaranjan Das, it set the stage for future political movements and strategies against British rule.
 
• The party's efforts to use legislative councils as platforms for resistance inspired later political initiatives and reforms.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Zaid crop (grown in the Zaid season)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Watermelon**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• **Zaid crops** are crops that are grown during the **Zaid season**, which falls in between the **Rabi and Kharif crop seasons**. This season typically spans from **March to June** in India.
 
• These crops require **hot, dry weather for growth** and a shorter growing cycle compared to Rabi and Kharif crops. They are cultivated in areas with sufficient **irrigation facilities** to meet water requirements.
 
• **Watermelon** is a classic example of a Zaid crop. It thrives well in the hot weather of the Zaid season and requires a **short cropping cycle**, making it suitable for cultivation during this time.
 
• Other examples of Zaid crops include **muskmelon, cucumber, bitter gourd, and fodder crops**. These crops are generally consumed as fruits or vegetables and provide nutritional benefits.
 
• The other options provided in the question, such as **Rice, Cotton, and Wheat**, are not Zaid crops. These belong to either the Rabi or Kharif crop categories (explained further in the "Additional Information" section).
 
• **Rice:** A Kharif crop grown during the monsoon season (**June to October**).
 
• **Cotton:** Another Kharif crop grown in warm and humid conditions during the same season as rice.
 
• **Wheat:** A Rabi crop that requires cool weather and is grown during the winter season (**November to March**).
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Watermelon.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

__
 
• **Zaid Crops:**

 
 
• **Definition:** Zaid crops are grown in the **short season** between Rabi and Kharif seasons (**March to June**).
 
• **Climate Requirements:** These crops require **high temperatures** and **longer daylight hours** for their growth.
 
• **Examples:** Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, bitter gourd, and pumpkin are popular Zaid crops.
 
• **Applications:** Zaid crops provide fruits and vegetables during the summer months and contribute to **food security** and **nutritional needs**.
 
 
 
• **Kharif Crops:**
 
 
• **Definition:** These crops are sown with the onset of the monsoon (**June**) and harvested by **October**.
 
• **Examples:** Rice, maize, cotton, jowar, and bajra are prominent Kharif crops.
 
• **Climate Requirements:** These crops require **warm, wet weather** and are highly dependent on monsoon rains.
 
 
 
• **Rabi Crops:**
 
 
• **Definition:** These crops are grown during the winter season, typically sown in **November** and harvested in **March**.
 
• **Examples:** Wheat, mustard, barley, and peas are common Rabi crops.
 
• **Climate Requirements:** Rabi crops require **cool weather** for germination and growth and **warm weather** for harvesting.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__** 

 
• **Importance of Zaid Crops:**

 
 
• They fill the gap between Rabi and Kharif seasons, ensuring **continuous agricultural activity** and a **steady food supply**.
 
• Provide an additional source of income to farmers during the lean period.
 
 
 
• **Irrigation Dependency:**
 
 
• As Zaid crops are grown in summer, they rely heavily on **irrigation facilities** for water supply.
 
• Regions with well-established irrigation systems, such as **Punjab, Haryana, and Western Uttar Pradesh**, are ideal for Zaid crop cultivation.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Watermelon:**
 
 
• Watermelon is a **nutrient-rich fruit** that provides **hydration** and essential **vitamins**, making it a popular summer fruit.
 
• It is widely cultivated in India, especially in states like **Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu**.

questions.question: Which of the following is the oldest High Court in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Calcutta High Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Calcutta High Court** is the **oldest High Court** in India. It was established in **1862** under the **Indian High Courts Act of 1861**.
 
• The High Court is located in **Kolkata (Calcutta)**, West Bengal, and serves as the **principal civil and criminal court** for the state.
 
• The establishment of the Calcutta High Court marked the **beginning of a structured judicial system** in India under British rule.
 
• The court's jurisdiction extends to **West Bengal and the Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.**
 
• The first Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court was **Sir Barnes Peacock**.
 
• **Delhi High Court**, established in **1966**, is not the oldest High Court in India. Hence, option 2 is incorrect.
 
• **Allahabad High Court**, established in **1866**, is one of the oldest but not the oldest High Court. Hence, option 3 is incorrect.
 
• **Patna High Court**, established in **1916**, is not the oldest High Court. Hence, option 4 is incorrect.
 
• ***Therefore, the correct answer is Calcutta High Court.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indian High Courts Act, 1861:**

 
 
• This act was passed by the British Parliament to establish High Courts in India, replacing the earlier Supreme Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
 
• The act led to the establishment of **Calcutta High Court** (1862), followed by the High Courts of Bombay and Madras.
 
 
 
• **Role of High Courts in India:**
 
 
• High Courts are the **highest judicial authorities** at the state level, having original and appellate jurisdiction over civil and criminal cases.
 
• They also have the power to interpret the **Constitution** and enforce **fundamental rights** under Article 226.
 
 
 
• **Prominent Features of Calcutta High Court:**
 
 
• The court's building is an architectural marvel, modeled after the **Cloth Hall in Ypres, Belgium.**
 
• It has jurisdiction over cases involving the **Indian Constitution**, civil disputes, criminal offenses, and public interest litigation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Major High Courts:**

 
 
• **Bombay High Court** and **Madras High Court** were established in **1862** along with the Calcutta High Court, but Calcutta High Court remains the oldest by precedence.
 
• **Allahabad High Court**, though established later in **1866**, has played a crucial role in Indian legal history.
 
 
 
• **Judicial System Evolution:**
 
 
• The establishment of High Courts marked the beginning of a **structured legal framework** in colonial India.
 
• Post-independence, High Courts continue to be a significant part of the Indian judiciary, ensuring justice at the state level.

questions.question: Where did the infamous Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place in 1919?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Amritsar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Event – The Jallianwala Bagh Massacre occurred on 13 April 1919 in the public garden known as Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. It was a turning point in modern Indian history.
 
• Location – Jallianwala Bagh is a narrow, enclosed garden situated a short distance from the Golden Temple in the city of Amritsar, in the present-day state of Punjab, India. The location meant many civilians were gathered for a peaceful meeting and for the festival of Baisakhi.
 
• Cause / Context – The firing followed protests against the Rowlatt Act (1919) and colonial arrests; public outrage and mass demonstrations had intensified across Punjab. The meeting at Jallianwala Bagh was to protest recent arrests and to show solidarity.
 
• Perpetrator – Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to block exits and open fire without warning. This use of force against an unarmed crowd was widely condemned.
 
• Casualties & Numbers – Official British figures reported around 379 dead and over 1,200 wounded; Indian estimates were much higher. The incident’s human cost remains a key fact used to illustrate colonial repression.
 
• Immediate Aftermath – Martial law was imposed in parts of Amritsar. The event led to the Hunter Commission (1919) inquiry; while Dyer was censured by some bodies and praised by others, public opinion in India turned decisively against British rule.
 
• Long-term Significance – The massacre accelerated the shift from moderate petitioning to mass national movements; leaders like Mahatma Gandhi intensified campaigns of non-cooperation and civil disobedience. The event is widely cited as a catalyst in the growth of the Indian independence movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Amritsar **

questions.question: With which country does India share its largest international border?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bangladesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India shares its largest international border with Bangladesh**, which spans a length of approximately **4,096.7 kilometers**. This makes it the longest land boundary that India shares with any neighboring country.
 
• The India-Bangladesh border runs across multiple Indian states, including **West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram**. These states are geographically adjacent to Bangladesh.
 
• The border is marked by rivers, plains, hills, and densely populated regions. This diverse geography adds complexity to border management and security.
 
• The India-Bangladesh border has been a point of cooperation and contention historically. Both countries have worked together on issues like border management, trade, and resolving disputes, such as the **Land Boundary Agreement (LBA) of 2015**.
 
• The **Land Boundary Agreement (LBA)** was a significant milestone in resolving the longstanding boundary disputes between the two nations. It facilitated the exchange of **enclaves** and simplified border demarcation.
 
• Bangladesh gained independence from Pakistan in **1971**, and since then, India and Bangladesh have shared a long and complex border history.
 
• **Hence, the correct answer is Bangladesh.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Details about the India-Bangladesh Border:**

 
 
• **Length:** The total length of the India-Bangladesh border is approximately **4,096.7 kilometers**, making it the fifth-longest land border in the world.
 
• **States sharing the border:** The Indian states bordering Bangladesh are West Bengal (the largest share), Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
 
• **Geographical Features:** The border passes through diverse terrains, including rivers like the **Padma** and the **Brahmaputra**, forests, and hilly areas.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Land Boundary Agreement (LBA):**
 
 
• The **Land Boundary Agreement (2015)** resolved disputes over 162 enclaves: 111 Indian enclaves in Bangladesh and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves in India.
 
• The agreement ensured smoother border management and improved cross-border relations.
 
 
 
• **India's Other Borders:**
 
 
• India shares borders with **seven countries**: Bangladesh, Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, and Afghanistan (via PoK).
 
• **Second-largest border:** India’s second-largest international border is with China, spanning approximately **3,488 kilometers**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Smuggling:** The porous nature of the India-Bangladesh border makes it vulnerable to illegal activities such as smuggling of goods, drugs, and cattle.
 
• **Cross-border migration:** Historical and economic factors have led to significant migration across the border, sometimes straining bilateral relations.
 
 
 
• **Security Measures:**
 
 
• **Border fencing:** India has constructed fences along large sections of the border to curb illegal infiltration and smuggling.
 
• **Border Security Force (BSF):** The BSF is responsible for guarding the India-Bangladesh border and ensuring its security.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The Vice-President of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The Attorney-General of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The President of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
The Prime Minister of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Vice-President of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Vice-President of India is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:** According to **Article 64** of the **Indian Constitution**, the Vice-President of India acts as the **ex officio Chairman** of the **Rajya Sabha** (Council of States). The Vice-President presides over the meetings of the Rajya Sabha and ensures its smooth functioning. *This statement is correct.*
 
• **The Attorney-General of India is not the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:** The Attorney-General is the highest law officer in India and provides legal advice to the Government of India but has no legislative or presiding role in the Rajya Sabha. *This statement is incorrect.*
 
• **The President of India is not the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:** The President is the constitutional head of the country and does not preside over any House of Parliament. However, the President summons and prorogues sessions of both Houses of Parliament. *This statement is incorrect.*
 
• **The Prime Minister of India is not the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:** The Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers and leads the executive branch of the Government of India. The Prime Minister is not associated with presiding over the Rajya Sabha. *This statement is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Vice-President of India:**

 
 
• The Vice-President of India is elected under **Article 66** of the Indian Constitution by an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament.
 
• The Vice-President’s primary role is to act as the **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**, ensuring its smooth functioning and maintaining decorum in the House.
 
• The Vice-President also acts as the **acting President of India** in the event of the President’s death, resignation, or removal until a new President is elected.
 
 
 
• **Rajya Sabha:**
 
 
• The Rajya Sabha is the **Upper House** of Parliament, also known as the **Council of States**.
 
• It comprises **245 members**, of which 233 are elected by the legislative assemblies of the states and Union territories, and 12 are nominated by the President for their expertise in specific fields like literature, science, art, and social service.
 
• The Rajya Sabha is a **permanent House** and is not subject to dissolution, though one-third of its members retire every two years.
 
 
 
• **Attorney-General of India:**
 
 
• The Attorney-General is appointed under **Article 76** of the Constitution as the chief legal advisor to the Government of India.
 
• The Attorney-General is not a member of Parliament and does not have voting rights in any House, but they have the **right to speak in both Houses**.
 
 
 
• **President of India:**
 
 
• The President is the constitutional head of the State and acts under the provisions of the Constitution.
 
• The President’s role includes summoning and proroguing sessions of Parliament, dissolving the Lok Sabha, and addressing the Parliament at the commencement of the first session after each general election.
 
 
 
• **Prime Minister of India:**
 
 
• The Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers and the real executive authority of the Government of India.
 
• The Prime Minister advises the President on the appointment of other ministers and presides over Cabinet meetings.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of the Vice-President as Chairman:**

 
 
• The Vice-President as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is responsible for conducting its proceedings and ensuring discipline among the members.
 
• The Chairman does not vote in the first instance but exercises a **casting vote** in case of a tie.
 
 
 
• **Distinction between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha:**
 
 
• The Lok Sabha is the **Lower House** and directly represents the people, while the Rajya Sabha represents the **states and Union territories**.
 
• The Speaker is the presiding officer of the Lok Sabha, whereas the Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

questions.question: As of August 2020, in which of the following sectors, 100% FDI in equity in India is NOT permitted as per India’s FDI Policy?

__

• **100% FDI is permitted in various sectors:** Sectors like **E-commerce activities, Single Brand Product Retail Trading, and Wholesale Trading** allow up to 100% foreign equity under automatic route. *Hence, these options are incorrect.*
 
• **Multi Brand Product Retail Trading:** In India, **100% FDI is NOT permitted in multi-brand retail trading**. The sector allows up to **51% FDI** under government approval route, with conditions like minimum investment in back-end infrastructure and sourcing from small-scale industries. *Hence, this option is correct.*
 
• **Government Restrictions on Multi-brand Retail:** The restrictions aim to protect domestic retailers and small businesses while facilitating foreign investment in infrastructure development.
 
• Other sectors such as **Wholesale Trading** and **E-commerce Activities** are open to 100% FDI under automatic routes, making them favorable for international businesses. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **FDI in Multi Brand Retail Trading:**

 
 
• **51% FDI:** Multi-brand retail trading allows up to **51% foreign investment**, subject to government approval and compliance with specific conditions.
 
• **Conditions for FDI:** Investors must allocate at least **50% of the investment** in back-end infrastructure and source **30% of goods** locally from micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
 
 
 
• **E-commerce Activities:**
 
 
• **100% FDI:** E-commerce activities in India are open to **100% FDI** under the automatic route, encouraging global e-commerce giants to invest in the country.
 
• **Example:** Companies like **Amazon** and **Flipkart** have utilized this policy to expand their operations in India.
 
 
 
• **Single Brand Product Retail Trading:**
 
 
• **100% FDI:** Single-brand retail trading allows **100% foreign investment**, with 49% under the automatic route and the remainder subject to government approval.
 
• **Example:** Brands like **Apple** and **IKEA** have leveraged this policy to establish stores in India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of FDI Policies:**

 
 
• **Boost for Economy:** FDI policies aim to attract foreign investment, which contributes to **economic growth, employment generation, and infrastructure development**.
 
• **Protection of Domestic Interests:** Restrictions on multi-brand retail trading safeguard **small retailers and domestic businesses** from foreign competition.
 
 
 
• **Key Developments:**
 
 
• **2012:** The Indian government allowed **51% FDI** in multi-brand retail trading under specific conditions to balance foreign investment and domestic concerns.
 
• **Example:** Companies like **Walmart** have entered the Indian market, complying with government regulations and contributing to infrastructure development.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi started the Salt March on 12 March 1930 from:

__
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi** initiated the famous **Salt March** on **12 March 1930** to protest against the oppressive British salt tax.
 
• The Salt March, also known as the **Dandi March**, started from the **Sabarmati Ashram** in **Ahmedabad, Gujarat**.
 
• The march covered a distance of approximately **240 miles (390 km)** to the coastal village of **Dandi**, where Gandhi broke the salt laws by producing salt from seawater. *Hence, the correct answer is Sabarmati.*
 
• **Sabarmati Ashram** was the residence of Mahatma Gandhi from **1917 to 1930**. It served as the base for his many campaigns of civil disobedience.
 
• The Salt March was a significant event in the **Indian independence movement**, showcasing the power of non-violent resistance and mass mobilization.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Sabarmati Ashram:**

 
 
• Located on the banks of the **Sabarmati River** in Ahmedabad, this ashram was established by **Mahatma Gandhi** in **1917**.
 
• It served as the **headquarters of the Indian freedom struggle** and was a hub for various social and political activities led by Gandhi.
 
• The ashram remains a symbol of peace and non-violence and is preserved as a museum today.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Salt March:**
 
 
• The Salt March was a key event in the **Civil Disobedience Movement** against British rule.
 
• It was an act of defiance against the **British monopoly on salt**, which forced Indians to buy heavily taxed salt.
 
• The march garnered significant **national and international attention**, highlighting the Indian independence struggle on the global stage.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Champaran:** Known for Gandhi’s first major involvement in the Indian independence struggle in **1917**, focusing on the plight of indigo farmers.
 
• **Sevagram:** Gandhi’s ashram near Wardha, Maharashtra, established in **1936**, after leaving Sabarmati Ashram.
 
• **Santiniketan:** Founded by **Rabindranath Tagore** in Bengal, it is known for its cultural and educational significance, not associated with the Salt March.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Legacy of the Salt March:**

 
 
• The Salt March became a **symbol of resistance** against British colonial rule and inspired numerous movements globally.
 
• It demonstrated the power of **non-violent civil disobedience** as a tool for achieving political and social change.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Independence Movement:**
 
 
• The march united people from different regions, classes, and communities in India, fostering a sense of **national solidarity**.
 
• It paved the way for the **Second Round Table Conference** in London in **1931**, where Gandhi represented the Indian National Congress.

questions.question: Rabi crops are generally harvested in:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**March-June**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rabi crops** are sown during the **winter season**, typically from October to December, and harvested in the **spring or early summer months**, usually between **March and June**.
 
• These crops require a cool climate for growth and relatively **warmer weather during their harvesting period**.
 
• Rabi crops include **wheat, barley, mustard, gram**, and peas. These crops are integral to the agricultural economy of countries like India. *Hence, the correct option is March-June.*
 
• The sowing of Rabi crops typically starts after the end of the **monsoon season**, as the soil retains sufficient moisture. This helps in the germination of seeds and supports the initial growth stages.
 
• In India, Rabi crops are cultivated in regions with suitable climatic conditions and significant irrigation facilities due to low rainfall during their growth period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Rabi Crops:**

 
 
• Rabi crops are grown during the **dry season** (winter) and require irrigation due to low rainfall.
 
• The term "Rabi" originates from Arabic, meaning "spring," as these crops are harvested in the spring season.
 
• Examples of Rabi crops are **wheat, barley, mustard, gram**, and **peas**. They are mainly grown in regions with **moderate winters**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Kharif Crops:**
 
 
• Unlike Rabi crops, **Kharif crops** are sown during the rainy season (June to September) and harvested in the autumn months.
 
• **Kharif crops** include rice, maize, cotton, and groundnut.
 
• The major difference is that Kharif crops rely on **monsoon rainfall**, while Rabi crops depend on **irrigation**.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Rabi Crop Growth:**
 
 
• **Temperature:** Rabi crops need cool temperatures for germination and growth but warmer conditions for harvesting.
 
• **Moisture:** Adequate soil moisture left after the monsoon season is critical for Rabi crops.
 
• **Irrigation:** Since rainfall is scarce during winter, irrigation plays a vital role in the cultivation of Rabi crops.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Geographical Distribution:**

 
 
• Rabi crops are widely grown in **northern India**, including states like **Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Bihar**, due to favorable winter conditions.
 
• These regions have well-established irrigation systems that support Rabi crop cultivation.
 
 
 
• **Economic Importance:**
 
 
• Rabi crops like wheat and mustard are significant contributors to **India's agricultural economy**, providing staple food and raw materials for industries.
 
• The production of Rabi crops influences **food security** and the livelihoods of millions of farmers.

• The **SI unit of energy** is the **Joule**, denoted as "**J**".
 
• **Energy** is defined as the capacity to do work, and the Joule is used to measure this capacity in the **International System of Units (SI)**.
 
• One Joule is equal to the amount of energy transferred when a force of **1 Newton** is applied over a distance of **1 meter** in the direction of the force. Mathematically:

 **1 Joule = 1 Newton × 1 meter**.
 
• Other options such as Kilo Watt, Horse Power, and Newton are not correct because they represent different physical quantities, not energy:

 - **Kilo Watt** measures power (rate of energy transfer).

 - **Horse Power** is also a unit of power.

 - **Newton** measures force.
 
• The Joule is named after the English physicist **James Prescott Joule**, who made significant contributions to the study of energy and thermodynamics.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Joule (J):**

 
 
• The Joule is a derived unit in the SI system, expressed as **kg·m²/s²**.
 
• It is used across various domains of physics, including **mechanics, thermodynamics, and electricity**.
 
• Examples:
 
 
• When a current of **1 ampere** flows through a resistance of **1 ohm** for **1 second**, the energy dissipated is **1 Joule**.
 
• Lifting a mass of **102 grams** (approximately 1 Newton of weight) by **1 meter** requires 1 Joule of energy.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Kilo Watt (kW):**
 
 
• It is a unit of power, not energy. Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
 
• 1 kW equals **1000 Watts**, where 1 Watt = 1 Joule/second.
 
• Applications: Measuring electrical power consumption (e.g., electricity bills are calculated in **Kilo Watt-hours**).
 
 
 
• **Horse Power (HP):**
 
 
• Horse Power is another unit of power commonly used to measure the power of engines.
 
• 1 HP = **745.7 Watts**.
 
• Applications: Used in the automobile industry to describe the power of vehicles' engines.
 
 
 
• **Newton (N):**
 
 
• Newton is the SI unit of force, not energy.
 
• 1 Newton is the force required to accelerate a mass of **1 kilogram** at a rate of **1 meter per second squared**.
 
• Applications: Used in mechanics to measure forces acting on objects.

• **Energy Conversion:**

 
 
• Energy can be converted from one form to another. For example, chemical energy in fuel converts to mechanical energy in engines.
 
• In these conversions, the unit of energy remains consistent, and the Joule is a universally accepted standard.
 
 
 
• **Practical Applications:**
 
 
• **Electrical Appliances:** Energy consumption is measured in **Joules or Watt-hours**. For instance, a 60-Watt bulb consumes **216,000 Joules** in one hour.
 
• **Heat Energy:** In thermodynamics, heat energy is expressed in Joules or calories (1 calorie = 4.184 Joules).
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• **James Prescott Joule** (1818–1889) established the mechanical equivalence of heat, showing that heat and mechanical work are forms of energy.
 
• This discovery laid the foundation for the **first law of thermodynamics**.

• On **September 1, 2017**, India’s **foreign exchange reserves** crossed the **$400 billion mark** for the first time. This was a significant milestone for India’s financial and economic standing globally.
 
• The reserves include foreign currency assets, gold reserves, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and the Reserve Tranche Position with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
 
• This milestone was achieved due to **consistent inflow of foreign investments**, robust exports, and careful management of economic policies by the government and the Reserve Bank of India.
 
• The growth in forex reserves is crucial for ensuring **economic stability**, managing exchange rate volatility, and supporting international trade and debt obligations.
 
• The reserves reflect the **strength of India’s external sector** and its ability to withstand global financial uncertainties. The $400 billion milestone marked India’s enhanced economic credibility globally.
 
• The correct date when India’s forex reserves reached the $400 billion mark for the first time is **Friday, September 1, 2017.**

• **Foreign Currency Assets (FCA):** These are the largest component of forex reserves and include major currencies like the US Dollar, Euro, Pound Sterling, and Japanese Yen.
 
• **Gold Reserves:** India holds physical gold as a part of its reserves to ensure diversification and stability against currency fluctuations.
 
• **Special Drawing Rights (SDRs):** These are international reserve assets created by the IMF to supplement member countries’ official reserves.
 
• **Reserve Tranche Position (RTP):** It represents India’s quota contribution to the IMF, which can be withdrawn if needed.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Forex Reserves:**
 
 
• Forex reserves provide a cushion against global economic shocks and currency volatility. They help maintain the **exchange rate stability** of the Indian Rupee.
 
• They are used for **international trade payments** and meeting external debt obligations.
 
• A higher reserve level enhances investor confidence and supports India’s creditworthiness globally.
 
• Reserves also provide a safety net during economic or geopolitical instability.
 
 
 
• **Historical Milestones of India’s Forex Reserves:**
 
 
• **1991:** During the economic crisis, India’s forex reserves were critically low, amounting to less than $1 billion.
 
• **2017:** Achieving $400 billion marked a significant improvement in India’s external sector strength.
 
• **2021:** India’s forex reserves crossed $600 billion for the first time due to increased foreign investments and export growth.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of RBI:**

 
 
• The Reserve Bank of India is responsible for maintaining and managing India’s forex reserves.
 
• RBI intervenes in the foreign exchange market to stabilize the Rupee and ensure orderly conditions.
 
 
 
• **Global Comparison:**
 
 
• India ranks among the top countries globally with high forex reserves, alongside nations like China, Japan, and Switzerland.

questions.question: On which date was the Goods and Services Tax (GST) implemented in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**July 2017**__.

__
 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** was implemented in **India** on **July 1, 2017**. It marked a significant reform in the indirect tax structure of the country.
 
• The implementation of GST replaced multiple indirect taxes such as **Value Added Tax (VAT), Service Tax, Central Excise Duty, and other local taxes** with one comprehensive tax mechanism.
 
• GST is governed by the **Goods and Services Tax Council**, which comprises representatives from both the central and state governments. Its objective is to ensure uniformity in tax rates and regulations across the country.
 
• **July 1** is celebrated as **GST Day** to commemorate the implementation of this landmark reform in the Indian taxation system.
 
• GST implementation aimed to bring about transparency, efficiency, and simplification in tax compliance for businesses and individuals.
 
• The GST structure is based on a **four-tier tax slab**: 5%, 12%, 18%, and 28%, depending on the type of goods and services.
 
• The GST regime introduced the concept of **Input Tax Credit (ITC)**, which allows businesses to claim credit for taxes paid on inputs, thereby preventing the cascading effect of taxes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Background of GST Implementation:**

 
 
• The concept of GST was first introduced in **2000** during the Vajpayee government, but it took several years of negotiations and discussions to achieve consensus among states.
 
• The **122nd Constitutional Amendment Bill** was passed in **2016**, paving the way for the implementation of GST.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of GST:**
 
 
• GST is a **destination-based tax**, meaning the tax is collected at the point of consumption rather than the point of origin.
 
• It is a **dual GST model**, where both the center and states levy taxes on goods and services. The components are **CGST (Central GST)**, **SGST (State GST)**, and **IGST (Integrated GST)**.
 
• GST has reduced the complexity of the Indian taxation system by subsuming a variety of central and state taxes into one unified system.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of GST:**
 
 
• It eliminates the cascading effect of taxes, making goods and services cheaper in the long run.
 
• GST has enhanced tax compliance and widened the tax base by bringing more businesses into the tax net.
 
• It promotes the idea of **‘One Nation, One Tax’** by unifying the indirect tax system across India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Challenges in GST Implementation:**

 
 
• The transition to GST posed challenges for businesses in terms of adapting to new compliance requirements and filing returns through the **Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN)**.
 
• Initial implementation faced criticism for technical glitches and multiple changes in tax rates.
 
 
 
• **Impact of GST:**
 
 
• GST has significantly boosted **tax revenue collection** for the government by improving compliance and reducing tax evasion.
 
• It has enhanced the ease of doing business in India by simplifying tax procedures and promoting a unified market.
 
• The **GST Council** continues to refine the system, addressing issues and ensuring its smooth functioning.

questions.question: Condensation is one of the processes in the water cycle. Which of the following statements is true about condensation?

options.text: Solid state is transferred to liquid state
Vapour state is transferred to liquid state
Vapour state is transferred to solid state
Liquid state is transferred to solid state

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vapour state is transferred to liquid state**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Condensation is a process in the **water cycle** where the **water vapour** in the air cools down and changes into **liquid water.**
 
• This phenomenon occurs when the temperature drops and the air cannot hold the same amount of moisture, resulting in water particles forming droplets. **Hence, condensation involves the transfer of vapour state to liquid state.**
 
• Statement 1: "Solid state is transferred to liquid state" – This is incorrect as this process refers to **melting**, not condensation.
 
• Statement 2: "Vapour state is transferred to liquid state" – This is correct because condensation specifically describes this transformation.
 
• Statement 3: "Vapour state is transferred to solid state" – This is incorrect as this process refers to **deposition**, not condensation.
 
• Statement 4: "Liquid state is transferred to solid state" – This is incorrect as this process is called **freezing**, not condensation.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Vapour state is transferred to liquid state.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Condensation Process:**

 
 
• Condensation occurs when **water vapour cools** down and turns into liquid. For example, clouds are formed due to condensation.
 
• This process plays a crucial role in the **water cycle**, as it facilitates the formation of rain, snow, and other forms of precipitation.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Condensation:**
 
 
• Condensation is essential for **maintaining Earth's water balance**. It ensures that water vapour returns to the surface in the form of precipitation.
 
• It also plays a vital role in **regulating Earth's temperature.** For example, when water condenses, heat is released into the environment, influencing weather and climate patterns.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Condensation:**
 
 
• **Example:** Condensation is used in **industrial applications** such as distillation, refrigeration, and the creation of pure water through desalination processes.
 
• In daily life, condensation can be observed as **dew** forming on grass or water droplets on a cold glass of water.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key characteristics of other processes:**

 
 
• Melting refers to the conversion of a **solid into a liquid state**. For instance, ice melting into water.
 
• Freezing is the process where a **liquid turns into a solid**, such as water freezing to form ice.
 
• Deposition is a unique process where **vapour directly transforms into a solid** state, such as frost forming on cold surfaces.
 
 
 
• **Role in the water cycle:**
 
 
• Condensation, along with evaporation and precipitation, is a key component of the **water cycle** that ensures the movement of water through Earth's systems.
 
• This process helps maintain the **hydrological balance**, which is critical for sustaining life on Earth.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions can cause sodium deficiency?
questions.solution:

__
 
• **Sodium deficiency (Hyponatremia)** occurs when the body’s sodium levels drop below normal. Sodium is a key electrolyte responsible for maintaining fluid balance and proper muscle and nerve function.
 
• **Diarrhea:** Diarrhea causes excessive loss of fluids and electrolytes, including sodium, from the body. It leads to dehydration and can result in sodium deficiency if the fluid and electrolyte loss is not replenished adequately. *Hence, this is correct.*
 
• **Mental health disorders like dementia :** While dementia affects cognitive abilities, it does not directly lead to sodium deficiency. Sodium imbalance is not a direct symptom of dementia. 
 
• **Low blood pressure:** Although sodium is essential for maintaining blood pressure, low sodium levels (hyponatremia) do not directly cause chronic hypotension. However, acute drops in sodium can lead to temporary reductions in blood pressure. 
 
• **High blood pressure :** High sodium intake is usually linked to hypertension (high blood pressure), not deficiency. Sodium deficiency does not cause hypertension. 
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is dast.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sodium’s role in the body:**

 
 
• **Sodium (Na):** An essential electrolyte that helps regulate water balance, blood pressure, and nerve and muscle functions. The normal sodium level in the blood is between **135–145 mmol/L.**
 
• Sodium is primarily obtained through dietary sources such as **table salt (sodium chloride), canned foods, and processed snacks.**
 
 
 
• **Causes of sodium deficiency:**
 
 
• **Diarrhea and vomiting:** These conditions result in significant loss of fluids and electrolytes, including sodium.
 
• **Excessive sweating:** Sodium is lost through sweat during intense physical activity or high temperatures.
 
• **Kidney diseases:** Certain kidney disorders impair the body’s ability to retain sodium.
 
• **Medications:** Diuretics and certain drugs can lead to sodium depletion.
 
 
 
• **Symptoms of sodium deficiency:**
 
 
• Fatigue, muscle cramps, confusion, headache, and severe cases may lead to seizures or coma.
 
 
 
• **Preventive measures:**
 
 
• Stay hydrated and replenish electrolytes during diarrhea, vomiting, or heavy sweating using **oral rehydration solutions (ORS).**
 
• Consume a balanced diet with adequate sodium levels as recommended by health guidelines.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Diarrhea and sodium loss:**

 
 
• Diarrhea causes significant loss of fluids and electrolytes, making it crucial to address sodium depletion promptly to avoid severe complications like **dehydration and hyponatremia.**
 
• The use of **ORS (oral rehydration solutions)** is widely recommended by health organizations such as the **World Health Organization (WHO)** to combat sodium loss during diarrheal episodes.
 
 
 
• **Global impact:**
 
 
• Diarrhea is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among children under **5 years**, especially in developing countries.
 
• Efforts like **UNICEF's diarrhea management programs** emphasize educating communities on proper rehydration techniques.
